s1.quote: Ismene, sister of my blood and heart,
s1.note: The Greek first line is almost untranslatable: ὦ κοινὸν αὐτάδελφον Ἰσμήνης κάρα (l. 1), word for word 'O shared, very-own-sibling head of Ismene'. Three kinship terms are stacked before the verb arrives: κοινὸν (_koinon_, 'held in common'), αὐτάδελφον (_autadelphon_, 'own sibling, sibling of the selfsame womb'), and κάρα (_kara_, 'head', a way of saying 'dear person'). Storr unpacks the knot into 'blood and heart', which is graceful but loosens it; the Greek says, more strangely, that Ismene is the same stuff as the speaker. In this family, where a mother is also a grandmother, insisting on closeness of blood is not a simple compliment. Hold on to the line: by the end of this scene the 'shared' sister will have been told she is an enemy.

s1.quote: See’st thou how Zeus would in our lives fulfill
s1.note: Storr's 'our lives' hides a piece of grammar that matters. Greek has a dual number, used for exactly two of something, and Antigone uses it here: νῷν ἔτι ζώσαιν (l. 3, _noin eti zosain_, 'for the two of us still living'). The sisters are a pair, the surviving pair, set against the dead pair of brothers. Watch what happens to this form. Antigone uses it once more at l. 21, Ismene goes on using it all through her long speech, and after Ismene refuses Antigone does not use it of the two of them again.

s1.quote: The weird of Oedipus, a world of woes!
s1.note: 'Weird' is a noun, the old word for fate or doom, as in the Weird Sisters. The Greek is plainer, 'the evils that come from Oedipus', and the word κακῶν (_kakon_, 'evils') ends three lines in her first ten (ll. 2, 6, 10). Her first thought is that she lives inside an inheritance, and the elders will sing the same idea back at her in [[s6|the Second Stasimon]]. Notice that she names Zeus as the one bringing it to completion: the gods are in her mouth from the second line, though not yet as her allies.

s1.quote: For what of pain, affliction, outrage, shame,
s1.note: Four negatives in the Greek (ll. 4-5), and the second is a famous difficulty: the manuscripts give ἄτης ἄτερ (_ates ater_, 'without ruin'), which makes her say the opposite of what she means, and editors either emend or assume the string of negatives has tangled. Storr's 'affliction' steps over the problem. What matters for us is that ἄτης is the play's first use of _ate_, the ruin or blind folly that the gods send on a house, and it is the governing word of [[s6]]. The last of the four, ἄτιμόν (_atimon_, 'without honour'), starts another thread: honour and dishonour are how both Antigone and Creon will describe what is done to the brothers.

s1.quote: Made by our Captain-General to the State,
s1.note: Storr's odd title is faithful. She calls Creon τὸν στρατηγὸν (l. 8, _ton strategon_, 'the general'), not king, and what he has issued is a κήρυγμα (_kerygma_, 'a herald's proclamation'), not a law. To an Athenian audience _strategos_ was an elected military office, the one Pericles held; an ancient note prefixed to the play says Sophocles himself was made general on the strength of it. So her first description of Creon shrinks him to a wartime commander giving orders, addressed πανδήμῳ πόλει ('to the whole people, the city'). Whether the edict is a law or only an order is the question she will argue in [[s5]], and she has pre-judged it in her vocabulary here.

s1.quote: Or art thou deaf when friends are banned as foes?
s1.note: Here is the pair of words the whole play turns on: φίλους (_philous_) and ἐχθρῶν (_echthron_), l. 10. _Philos_ is not 'friend' in our sense; it means one's own, kin and those bound to you, whether or not you like them. The Greek says literally 'evils of enemies marching on our own people', and it can mean either 'treatment fit for enemies' or 'evils coming from our enemies'. Storr picks the first. Either way, Antigone's opening move is to say that someone has put a _philos_ in the wrong category, and Creon will reply in [[s3]] that it is the city that decides who counts as a _philos_ at all.

s1.quote: To me, Antigone, no word of friends
s1.note: Ismene picks up the word at once: φίλων (l. 11). But she hears it as 'news about those we love', glad or painful, where Antigone meant a claim. That small mishearing is the scene in miniature. The sisters use the same vocabulary of family throughout and never mean quite the same thing by it.

s1.quote: Were reft of our two brethren in one day
s1.note: Ismene counts. In two lines of Greek (ll. 13-14) she has 'two' twice, 'one' once and 'double' once: δυοῖν ἀδελφοῖν ('of two brothers', in the dual), then 'we two', then 'one day', then διπλῇ χερί ('by a double hand'). Storr's 'double fratricide' names the deed; the Greek only gives the paired hands. This is a family that comes in twos, and the arithmetic of pairs runs right through her big speech below.

s1.quote: Our Argive leaguers fled, no later news
s1.note: 'Leaguers' are besiegers. The Greek fixes the time: the army went 'in this very night' (l. 16), so the scene is played in the last dark before dawn, and the Chorus will enter greeting the sunrise in [[s2]]. Her closing word is stronger than Storr's 'deject': ἀτωμένη (l. 17, _atomene_), 'struck by ruin', the verb of _ate_ again within twenty lines of its first appearance.

s1.quote: Beyond the gates to breathe it in thine ear.
s1.note: Staging first: two unmarried girls of the royal house are standing outside the courtyard doors before daybreak, which is not where such girls belong, and Creon will say so later. Antigone has brought her sister out 'so that you alone might hear' (l. 19). The tutor's question is why the woman who will shortly demand that her deed be shouted to the whole town begins with secrecy. I think the answer is that here she is recruiting, and once the recruit refuses there is nothing left that secrecy could protect.

s1.quote: What is it? Some dark secret stirs thy breast.
s1.note: Ismene's verb (_kalchainousa_, l. 20) comes from the word for the purple-fish and means to go dark and troubled like a sea before a storm. Storr's 'dark' and 'stirs' between them keep the picture. It tells us how Antigone looks to someone who knows her: she is visibly brooding before she has said a word about burial.

s1.quote: What but the thought of our two brothers dead,
s1.note: The first word of her answer in Greek is τάφου (l. 21, _taphou_, 'burial'), and the line has two duals side by side: νῷν ('of us two') and the two brothers. Two sisters, two brothers. It is the last time Antigone includes Ismene in that grammatical pair. Creon is also named here for the first time, as the subject of the sentence.

s1.quote: The one by Creon graced with funeral rites,
s1.note: The Greek sets two participles against each other: προτίσας ('having honoured above') and ἀτιμάσας ('having dishonoured'), l. 22. She describes the edict as a distribution of honour, _time_, and that is exactly how Creon will describe it himself in [[s3]]. On this point the two agree. They differ over who has the right to hand honour out, and whether the dead can be ranked by the city.

s1.quote: With obsequies that use and wont ordain,
s1.note: The text of ll. 23-24 is uncertain, but the words that survive are δίκης ('justice') and νόμου (_nomou_, 'law, custom'). This is the first occurrence of _nomos_ in the play, and it belongs to Antigone, about burial, in the sense of settled custom; Storr's 'use and wont' is exactly right. Only afterwards does the word get attached to Creon's order (Ismene does it at l. 59). So the reader meets _nomos_ meaning 'what is always done for the dead' before meeting it as 'what the ruler has decreed'. Notice also her 'as fame reports' here and twice more below: she has the edict by hearsay.

s1.quote: Must leave him tombless and unwept, a feast
s1.note: Two privative adjectives side by side: ἄκλαυτον, ἄταφον (l. 29, _aklauton_, _ataphon_, 'unwept, unburied'), in that order, lament first. The ban is on mourning as well as on burial, and lament was the women's part in a funeral, so the edict falls on the sisters in a way it does not fall on the men of the city. The same kind of string comes back at the other end of her story: led to her tomb in [[s9]] she calls herself _aklautos_, _aphilos_, _anymenaios_, unwept, friendless, unwed.

s1.quote: For kites to scent afar and swoop upon.
s1.note: Storr's 'feast' in the line before is weaker than the Greek, which calls the body a γλυκὺν θησαυρὸν (ll. 29-30, _glykyn thesauron_, 'a sweet treasure-store') for the birds. A _thesauros_ is a hoard, something laid up; the corpse is a find. This is bitter and deliberate, and it is not her image alone. The birds return in [[s11]], where Teiresias reports that they are glutted with the dead man's flesh and will no longer give signs.

s1.quote: Of Creon, our most noble Creon, aimed
s1.note: τὸν ἀγαθὸν Κρέοντα (l. 31), 'the good Creon', and the adjective is pure sarcasm. _Agathos_ is the standard word of approval for a man of rank, so she is quoting the city's opinion of him back with a curl of the lip. Storr's 'most noble' gets the tone.

s1.quote: At thee and me, aye me too; and anon
s1.note: The edict was proclaimed to the townsmen (l. 27), yet she hears it as aimed at the two of them, and then adds 'I say, at me too' (l. 32). There are two ways to take the aside. Either it is incredulity (he imagines he can forbid me), or she already assumes Ismene will obey and she will not. I incline to the first, but both readings show the same thing: for her the decree is personal before it is political. The rest of the sentence prepares Creon's entrance in [[s3]]; he is on his way to say all this in person.

s1.quote: Whoe’er transgresses shall be stoned to death.
s1.note: The Greek word is δημόλευστον (l. 36, _demoleuston_), 'stoned by the people'. Stoning is the punishment in which the community itself does the killing, the proper end for a traitor. Creon will quietly exchange it for something private, a sealed cave, at the end of [[s7]]. I think the exchange tells us he has stopped trusting the community to throw.

s1.quote: If thou art worthy of thy blood or base.
s1.note: εὐγενὴς (l. 38, _eugenes_, 'well-born') against 'base daughter of a noble line'. Her ethic is the old aristocratic one, in which birth is an obligation and you show what you are by what you do. There is an irony she does not pause over: of all houses, this is the one where 'worthy of your blood' is a doubtful recommendation. Mark also πέφυκας ('you are by nature'). Ismene will answer with the same verb twice (ll. 62, 79): both sisters argue from nature, and reach opposite conclusions.

s1.quote: But how, my rash, fond sister, in such case
s1.note: Her address is ταλαῖφρον (l. 39, _talaiphron_), a compound meaning something like 'poor suffering mind', gentler than Storr's 'rash'. It is the first of the play's many words built on _phren_, the mind or wits. The next line, which Storr gives as 'make or mar', is in Greek 'by loosening or by tightening', the image of a knot. Ismene sees a tangle and asks what a pair of hands could do to it either way.

s1.quote: Say, wilt thou aid me and abet? Decide.
s1.note: Line-for-line exchange (stichomythia) begins here, and the pace changes. Antigone's line has two verbs with the same prefix: ξυμπονήσεις and ξυνεργάσει (l. 41), 'will you share the labour, will you share the deed'. 'With' is what she is asking for. Keep the prefix in mind, because the only 'with' Ismene will find to offer is at l. 85, and it is not the one wanted.

s1.quote: Lend me a hand to bear the corpse away.
s1.note: κουφιεῖς (l. 43, _kouphieis_, 'will you lift'), 'together with this hand', and the actor must hold up her own. The plan as first stated is to raise and carry the body, which is a two-person job and implies a real burial. Alone, all she can do is scatter dust and pour libations. That bears on the old puzzle of why there are two burials in [[s3]] and [[s5]]: what she manages by herself is from the start less than what she meant to do.

s1.quote: What, bury him despite the interdict?
s1.note: ἀπόρρητον πόλει (l. 44), 'a thing forbidden to the city', or possibly 'by the city'; the dative allows both. Either way Ismene says _polis_ where Antigone said Creon. To one sister the ban belongs to the community, to the other it is one man's order. That disagreement is never settled between them, and it is the same question Haemon will put to his father in [[s7]].

s1.quote: My brother, and, though thou deny him, thine
s1.note: The possessives carry it: 'mine at any rate, and yours' (l. 45). Storr's 'though thou deny him' is a little harsher than the Greek 'if you are unwilling'. Ancient commentators already suspected the following line of being an addition (the scholia report this from Didymus), which shows how compressed and abrupt the passage felt even then. I see no need to cut it.

s1.quote: betrayed a brother.
s1.note: The word is the one for treason (_prodousa_, l. 46), and she says she will not be 'caught' at it. That is pointed. Polyneices is the traitor in the city's account, the man who betrayed Thebes; she takes the city's gravest charge and turns it into the thing she would be guilty of if she obeyed. Loyalty to the city and loyalty to kin are already competing for the same vocabulary.

s1.quote: Wilt thou persist, though Creon has forbid?
s1.note: Storr drops Ismene's cry: σχετλία (l. 47, _schetlia_), 'hard, unflinching one', said with as much awe as reproach. Her addresses to her sister make a sequence worth following: 'poor mind' at l. 39, 'hard one' here, 'unhappy one' at l. 82. She is watching someone she loves move out of reach.

s1.quote: What right has he to keep me from my own?
s1.note: Her whole case in nine words, and it is not yet about heaven. The Greek is τῶν ἐμῶν (l. 48, _ton emon_), 'my own', plural and open: my own people, my own things. Literally 'he has no share in keeping me from what is mine'. The grand language of unwritten laws comes in [[s5]]; the possessive comes first. A tutor would ask whether the later argument is the reason for the act or its justification after the fact. This line is the evidence for the second view.

s1.quote: Bethink thee, sister, of our father’s fate,
s1.note: φρόνησον (l. 49, _phroneson_), 'think, be sensible'. This is the first appearance of _phronein_, the play's word for sound thinking, and it comes as a plea from Ismene. The same word is the play's last lesson: the closing lines of [[s13]] say that good sense is the chief part of happiness and is learned late. Everyone in between accuses someone else of lacking it. Ismene's speech is also the only long one in the scene, and it is an argument, laid out in order: father, then mother, third the brothers, and now us.

s1.quote: Blinded, himself his executioner.
s1.note: Three compounds of 'self' in six Greek lines: αὐτοφώρων (l. 51, sins 'self-detected'), αὐτουργῷ (l. 52, a hand 'working on its own'), αὐτοκτονοῦντε (l. 56, the brothers 'killing their own'). Storr catches most of them ('self-convinced', 'himself', 'self-slaughtered'). In this house everything is done by the family to the family. The series is leading somewhere: the Chorus will call Antigone _autonomos_, a law to herself, in [[s9]]. Note too that in this play Oedipus died hated and in disgrace; the consoling end at Colonus is a play Sophocles wrote decades later.

s1.quote: Think of his mother-wife (ill sorted names)
s1.note: διπλοῦν ἔπος (l. 53), 'a double word': one woman, two names, mother and wife. The doubles go on accumulating (double eyes at l. 51, double word here, two brothers on one day at l. 55). Then the manner of death: πλεκταῖσιν ἀρτάναισι (l. 54), 'with twisted nooses'. Ismene holds up Jocasta's hanging as the thing to avoid, and it is precisely the death Antigone will choose in the cave in [[s13]].

s1.quote: Self-slaughtered, both the slayer and the slain.
s1.note: The brothers are in the dual throughout ll. 55-57, as the sisters were, and the doom they worked on each other is κοινὸν (l. 57, _koinon_, 'shared'). That is the first word of the play's first line coming back. What Antigone offered Ismene as a bond, Ismene returns as a warning: the thing this family holds in common is a way of dying.

s1.quote: Bethink thee, sister, we are left alone;
s1.note: Here Ismene's use of the dual is at its most insistent: μόνα, νὼ, λελειμμένα (l. 58), 'alone, we two, left behind', all in the form for a pair. Her whole argument is the pair. She is not weighing one life against a principle; she is asking Antigone not to break up the last two. It is worth reading her speech as love before reading it as timidity.

s1.quote: If in defiance of the law we cross
s1.note: νόμου βίᾳ (l. 59), 'in violence to law'. Ismene grants the edict the name _nomos_ without hesitation, the name Antigone gave to burial custom at l. 24. What she fears to cross is ψῆφον τυράννων (l. 60), 'the vote of rulers'. _Psephos_ is the pebble dropped in an Athenian ballot, a civic word, oddly joined to _tyrannoi_, which in tragedy can mean simply 'kings' but never sounded quite neutral in Athens. Storr's 'a monarch's will' loses the vote.

s1.quote: A monarch’s will?—weak women, think of that,
s1.note: 'Weak' is Storr's. The Greek says only 'that we were born women': ἔφυμεν (l. 62, _ephymen_), the verb of nature and birth that Antigone used at l. 38. Antigone said nature obliges you to act as your blood requires; Ismene says nature has fixed what you are able to do. This is the first time gender is named in the play, and it is named by a woman as a boundary.

s1.quote: Not framed by nature to contend with men.
s1.note: The participle is dual again (l. 62): 'the two of us, not ones to fight against men'. Ismene states as a fact of nature the very thing Creon will keep repeating as a fear: that he must not be beaten by a woman, that while he lives no woman shall rule ([[s5]], [[s7]]). The play lets a woman say it first, gently, before a man says it with guards behind him.

s1.quote: Remember this too that the stronger rules;
s1.note: Read this carefully, because Ismene never says Creon is right. Her two reasons are that they are women and that they are ruled by people with more force. It is an argument from power only, and she follows it to its end: one must obey 'in this and in things more painful still'.

s1.quote: Therefore I plead compulsion and entreat
s1.note: She asks pardon of those under the earth, because, she says, she is being forced (ll. 65-66). So she concedes the main point. The dead have a claim, the claim is being denied, and she needs forgiveness for her part in denying it. The sisters do not disagree about what is right. They disagree about whether right can be done, and Antigone will treat that as no difference at all.

s1.quote: To overstep in aught the golden mean.
s1.note: Storr brings in the 'golden mean' and a rhyme to round the speech off. The Greek is blunter: περισσὰ πράσσειν (l. 68, _perissa prassein_), 'to do what is beyond the measure, to act out of one's place', has no νοῦν (_noun_, 'sense') in it. _Perissos_ means excessive, over and above, and Creon will use the same adjective with contempt at the end of [[s7]], calling reverence for the dead 'labour to excess'. Ismene means it kindly, but it is his word.

s1.quote: I urge no more; nay, wert thou willing still,
s1.note: A change of ground in two lines. Thirty lines ago she was asking; now she says that even if Ismene changed her mind she would not have her. The speed is the characterisation. Is it fair? Ismene has just asked the dead for pardon and has not said a word against the burial. But Antigone means it, and she keeps to it: when Ismene tries to share the guilt in [[s5]], she is refused in the same terms.

s1.quote: Go thine own way; myself will bury him.
s1.note: In the Greek the verb is held over to the start of the next line and stands alone: θάψω (l. 72, _thapso_), 'I will bury him', with an emphatic 'I' before it. The pair is finished. From this point every verb she uses for the deed is first person singular, and the dual she shared with Ismene at ll. 3 and 21 is gone.

s1.quote: How sweet to die in such employ, to rest,—
s1.note: Not 'sweet'. The word is καλόν (l. 72, _kalon_), 'fine, noble, beautiful', the adjective of the heroic code, and what is _kalon_ is θανεῖν, 'to die', doing this. Storr has turned a claim about honour into a feeling. Notice how early it comes: she has not yet touched the body and death is already the settled price. The phrase will be repeated to close her part in the scene at l. 97.

s1.quote: Sister and brother linked in love’s embrace—
s1.note: Storr elaborates. The Greek line is φίλη at one end and φίλου at the other with the verb κείσομαι between (l. 73): 'dear, I shall lie with him, with one who is dear'. 'Sister and brother' and 'embrace' are his. But he is responding to something real, because _keisomai_ is the verb for lying in a grave and also for lying beside a lover, and she uses it again three lines on. The strand that ends with her going to the tomb as to a bridal chamber in [[s9]] begins here.

s1.quote: A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth,
s1.note: The famous oxymoron: ὅσια (l. 74, _hosia_, 'holy things') followed by a participle (_panourgesasa_) from the word for a rogue, someone who will do anything. 'Having committed a holy crime', or 'having piously played the villain'. She knows it is a crime; she never pretends the law does not exist, only that something outranks it. Creon will use the noun from the same root for plain criminality in [[s3]]. 'Banned awhile on earth' is Storr's bridge to the next thought and is not in the Greek.

s1.quote: But by the dead commended; and with them
s1.note: Her reason is almost arithmetic: the time during which she must please those below (l. 75) is longer than the time she must please those here, because there she will lie for ever. This is her first justification, and it is about loyalty and duration, not law. It is a reckoning of advantage, though the word for gain, _kerdos_, is nowhere in this scene. Creon will assume in [[s3]] that gain is the only motive anyone could have for touching the body, and in [[s5]] she takes the word from him: to die before her time, she says, she counts as gain. The sum she does here is what she will mean by it.

s1.quote: Scorn, if thou wilt, the eternal laws of Heaven.
s1.note: Storr has borrowed 'eternal laws' from the great speech in [[s5]]; nothing so developed is here. The Greek says 'hold in dishonour what the gods hold in honour' (l. 77), with two _time_-words set against each other. It is the first time she claims the gods for her side, and she does it in a parting shot, by throwing at Ismene the verb she used of Creon at l. 22. Ismene is being moved into Creon's column.

s1.quote: I scorn them not, but to defy the State
s1.note: βίᾳ πολιτῶν (l. 79), 'in violence to the citizens'. Citizens, not Creon. And ἀμήχανος (_amechanos_), 'without resource, unable': she says she is by nature incapable of it. Remember the phrase. In the disputed lines of her last speech in [[s9]] Antigone herself says she acted 'in defiance of the citizens', in exactly these words. If that passage is genuine, she ends by accepting Ismene's description of what she did.

s1.quote: To lap my dearest brother in the grave.
s1.note: φιλτάτῳ (l. 81, _philtatoi_), the superlative of _philos_: 'dearest', most her own. The verb beside it means to heap up a mound, so she is still thinking of a proper tomb, more than she will be able to do. Storr's 'alone' in the line before has no word behind it in the Greek, though it is true enough to the sense.

s1.quote: O waste no fears on me; look to thyself.
s1.note: Literally 'set your own lot straight' (l. 83), with a verb built on _orthos_, 'upright'. Straightness is about to become Creon's favourite idea; his first speech in [[s3]] is full of a city set upright and a ship kept on an even keel. Here it is a sneer between sisters, and Ismene will give the word back in the last line of the scene.

s1.quote: But keep it close and secret, as will I.
s1.note: After 'in secret' the Greek adds 'and I likewise with you' (l. 85). That phrase is the 'with' Antigone asked for at l. 41, returned in the only form Ismene can manage. She will not share the work, but she will share the silence. It is an offer of complicity, and I think it is meant as a real gift.

s1.quote: O tell it, sister; I shall hate thee more
s1.note: ἐχθίων (l. 86, _echthion_), the comparative of _echthros_: 'you will be more of an enemy'. Storr's 'hate' makes it an emotion; the Greek is closer to a status. Ismene is being reclassified, in the same pair of terms Antigone opened with at l. 10. The 'own sibling' of line 1 is now measured on the scale of enemies.

s1.quote: If thou proclaim it not to all the town.
s1.note: κηρύξῃς (l. 87, _keryxeis_), 'proclaim as a herald', the verb behind Creon's κήρυγμα at l. 8. She wants her act published in the same way as his edict. This is what complicates any reading of her as a private mourner: secrecy would save her life and she treats the suggestion as an insult. And yet the first burial is done unseen, before the guards are awake. The deed and the declaration are not quite the same person.

s1.quote: Thou hast a fiery soul for numbing work.
s1.note: The Greek is a neat antithesis that 'numbing' blurs: θερμὴν ... καρδίαν over ψυχροῖσι (l. 88), 'a hot heart over cold things'. Cold things are chilling deeds, and also, plainly, the dead. It is the most exact thing anyone says about her in the scene. Her warmth is all directed at what is cold.

s1.quote: If thou succeed; but thou art doomed to fail.
s1.note: Storr leaves out the most interesting word. Ismene says ἀμηχάνων ἐρᾷς (l. 90): 'you are in love with the impossible'. The verb is from _eros_. Desire enters the play here, long before Haemon is mentioned, and its object is something that cannot be had. When the Chorus sing to Eros in [[s8]], the one who drives even the just mind off course, it is worth remembering that Ismene diagnosed it in her sister first.

s1.quote: When strength shall fail me, yes, but not before.
s1.note: She concedes the point about impossibility and makes it irrelevant. Her standard is effort, not result: she will stop when she physically cannot go on. It is a soldier's answer.

s1.quote: But, if the venture’s hopeless, why essay?
s1.note: θηρᾶν (l. 92, _theran_), 'to hunt': one should not hunt the impossible in the first place. This is the third use of the same root in fourteen lines (ll. 79, 90, 92), and it is Ismene's word for both herself and the task. Set it beside [[s4|the ode on man]], which praises the creature who is never without resource and who hunts and snares everything that lives. Ismene's vocabulary of helplessness is the ode's vocabulary turned inside out.

s1.quote: Sister, forbear, or I shall hate thee soon,
s1.note: Two more forms of _echthros_ in two lines: ἐχθαρεῖ (l. 93), 'you will be hated', and ἐχθρὰ (l. 94), 'an enemy' to the dead man, and justly. The verb with it is προσκείσει, 'you will lie beside', the same root as the κείσομαι of l. 73: Antigone will lie with him as one of his own, Ismene as his enemy. This is where I part from the reading that makes Antigone simply the voice of love. Her line in [[s5]], that she was born to join in loving and not in hating, is true of her towards the dead. Towards the living her division into friend and enemy is as hard as Creon's.

s1.quote: Say I am mad and give my madness rein
s1.note: 'Mad' overstates it. Her word is δυσβουλίαν (l. 95, _dysboulian_), 'bad counsel, poor judgement': 'leave me and the folly that is mine'. She takes Ismene's charge and wears it ironically. Good and bad counsel are words the play keeps for its ending: Teiresias calls good counsel the best possession in [[s11]], and the same noun she uses here is on Creon's lips, of himself, over his son's body in [[s13]].

s1.quote: To wreck itself; the worst that can befall
s1.note: What she will suffer is τὸ δεινὸν τοῦτο (l. 96), 'this terrible thing'. δεινὸν (_deinon_) is the word that opens [[s4|the ode on man]]: many things are _deina_, formidable, strange, terrible, and nothing more so than a human being. Its first use in the play is hers, about the consequence she is walking towards with her eyes open. Storr's 'the worst that can befall' flattens a word the audience is about to hear sung.

s1.quote: Is but to die an honorable death.
s1.note: καλῶς θανεῖν (l. 97), 'to die nobly', closing the ring opened at l. 72. These are her last words before she goes to do it, and they are about the manner of her death, not about her brother. A tutor would ask whether she gets what she asks for. A noose in a sealed cave is not obviously a noble death, and her own lament in [[s9]] suggests that by then she is not sure.

s1.quote: Have thine own way then; ’tis a mad endeavor,
s1.note: Her word is _anous_ (l. 99), 'without sense', the negative of the _nous_ Ismene appealed to at l. 68. She does not take it back. Storr marks the end of the scene with a rhyming couplet, as he often does; the Greek has no rhyme, only an antithesis balanced across the line.

s1.quote: Yet to thy lovers thou art dear as ever.
s1.note: 'Lovers' means simply her own people. The Greek is τοῖς φίλοις and then ὀρθῶς φίλη (l. 99): 'to your own, truly one of their own'. It can be taken two ways, 'truly dear to those who love you' or 'a true friend to those you love', and I think Ismene means both. She gives the last word on _philos_, and quietly includes herself among the _philoi_ just after being called an enemy. It goes unanswered. Storr's 'Exeunt' hides the staging: Antigone leaves by the side passage toward the plain and Ismene goes back into the house, by different ways.

s2.quote: Sunbeam, of all that ever dawn upon
s2.note: 'Ray of the sun' are the first words of the Chorus, fifteen old men of Thebes filing into the dancing-floor as the sisters leave it. Everything changes at once: dark to light, two voices to many, secrecy to public song, 'I' to 'we'. The elders know nothing of what we have just heard. They do not know of the edict, and they have no idea that the celebration they are beginning has already been undone.

s2.quote: Our seven-gated Thebes the brightest ray,
s2.note: The light is κάλλιστον (l. 100, _kalliston_), 'the most beautiful' ever to shine on Thebes. That is the superlative of the word Antigone has just used twice for her own death (ll. 72, 97). For her the beautiful thing is to die doing this; for the elders it is the morning on which the city is still standing. ἑπταπύλῳ ('seven-gated') starts a count of sevens that runs through the song (ll. 118, 141) and keeps the old story of the Seven against Thebes in the audience's mind.

s2.quote: O eye of golden day,
s2.note: More exactly 'eyelid': ἁμέρας βλέφαρον (l. 103, _hameras blepharon_). The day is opening its eye, which is a better picture of dawn than a staring 'eye'. And the day is χρυσέας, 'golden'. Remember the gold; it comes back at l. 130 on the other side, as the clanging gold of the enemy's pride.

s2.quote: How fair thy light o’er Dirce’s fountain shone,
s2.note: Dirce is the stream on the west side of Thebes, and with Ismenus on the east it stands for the city's own ground. Local water is how a Greek chorus says 'home'. Antigone will call on the same springs as witnesses when she is led away in [[s9]], so the landmark that opens the song of victory returns in the lament of the victory's casualty.

s2.quote: Far quicker than they came, the Argive force;
s2.note: The Greek is one long sentence in which the sunbeam itself drives the enemy off, as a rider would, 'with a sharper bridle': χαλινῷ (l. 107, _chalinoi_). And the enemy is singular. The whole army is 'the man from Argos', φῶτα (l. 106), a fugitive running headlong. Storr turns this into a plural 'force' and loses the oddity of an army imagined as a single body, which prepares the eagle that follows.

s2.quote: The argent shields, the host with scutcheons white.
s2.note: λεύκασπιν (l. 106, _leukaspin_), 'white-shielded'. The name Argos sounds like the Greek word for 'bright, white', and Storr's 'argent' is a clever way of keeping the play on words. The white shield then becomes the white wing of the eagle, 'of white snow', a few lines on (l. 114). The elders' picture of the enemy is all glare.

s2.quote: To vindicate fell Polyneices’ claim.
s2.note: 'Fell', cruel or deadly, is Storr's addition. What the Greek has is a pun on the name: Πολυνείκους (l. 110), 'Much-strife', roused by νεικέων (l. 111, _neikeon_, 'quarrels'). And the quarrels are ἀμφιλόγων (_amphilogon_), 'disputed, with something said on both sides'. In the legend the brothers were to share the throne and Eteocles kept it. So in the very song that celebrates his defeat, the elders' own adjective admits the traitor had a case.

s2.quote: Like to an eagle swooping low,
s2.note: The eagle comes screaming shrill, and this part is chanted in marching anapaests, a different rhythm from the sung stanzas, which Storr's layout does not show. The eagle is Zeus's own bird, yet Zeus will strike this one down. With the serpent of l. 125 it makes the omen from the Iliad, eagle against snake, in which the snake wins. And notice the birds. In the prologue birds were to feed on Polyneices (l. 29); here his army is the bird of prey. The punishment has been fitted to the image.

s2.quote: His spearmen raven at our seven gates.
s2.note: The eagle stands over the roofs ἀμφιχανὼν (l. 117, _amphichanon_), 'gaping all round' with spears for a beak, at the ἑπτάπυλον στόμα (l. 118), the 'seven-gated mouth' of the city. One mouth gapes at another. Storr's 'raven', to prey greedily, keeps the appetite but drops the mouths.

s2.quote: But ere a torch our crown of towers could burn,
s2.note: στεφάνωμα πύργων (l. 120), 'the garland of towers', the city wall seen as a wreath on a head. Storr's 'torch' is in Greek the god's name: 'pine-fed Hephaestus', Ἥφαιστον (l. 121), put for fire itself. Fire is the weapon the attackers brought and, a few lines on, the weapon Zeus uses on them.

s2.quote: Ere they had tasted of our blood, they turn
s2.note: γένυσιν (l. 120, _genysin_), 'jaws': before its jaws were filled with αἱμάτων, 'our blood'. The besieger is a carrion-eater. Creon takes this image straight into his decree in [[s3]], where Polyneices is the man who came to feed on kindred blood. The edict then answers the image exactly, by making him the thing that is fed on. I think the ode shows us where Creon's idea of a fitting penalty comes from: the city was already thinking in these pictures.

s2.quote: Forced by the Dragon; in their rear
s2.note: The Dragon, the serpent, is Thebes itself (l. 125). The city's first men sprang from the dragon's teeth that Cadmus sowed, so the Thebans are the serpent's brood, and the eagle has met its natural enemy. The Greek of this line is knotted and its exact construction disputed, but the sense is that the serpent was too hard an adversary to master. The dragon was sacred to Ares, whose din is heard in the same line and who appears in person at l. 139.

s2.quote: For Zeus who hates the braggart’s boast
s2.note: This is the theology of the song, and it is the play's ending stated in advance. Zeus ὑπερεχθαίρει (l. 128, _hyperechthairei_, 'hates beyond measure') the γλώσσης κόμπους (l. 127), 'boasts of a big tongue'. The Chorus's last words in [[s13]] say that the great words of the over-proud are paid for with great blows. They sing it here about an invader. They will say it there about Creon. Mark also the string of _hyper_-compounds in these lines (ll. 113, 128, 130): going over, hating over, arms carried too high.

s2.quote: Beheld that gold-bespangled host;
s2.note: χρυσοῦ καναχῆς (l. 130), 'of clanging gold', with ὑπεροπλίαις, 'in the arrogance of their arms'; the text is uncertain here but those words are clear enough. Storr drops the image just before it, that they came on 'in a great stream', ῥεύματι (l. 129). This is the second gold in the song. The first was the eyelid of day. One is the gods' light and the other is men's display, and Zeus looks at the second and throws fire.

s2.quote: As at the goal the paean they upraise,
s2.note: Storr's 'they' is wrong in an interesting way. The Greek turns singular: Zeus hurls fire at one man who was already at the top, starting to shout νίκην (l. 133, _niken_, 'victory'). This is Capaneus, who swore to burn Thebes whether Zeus willed it or not, and the ode never names him. His position on the wall is called βαλβίδων (l. 131, _balbidon_), the line on a race-course, so he is a runner struck down as he breasts the tape. The elders tell it as an athletic event with a divine referee.

s2.quote: To earthy from earth rebounding, down he crashed;
s2.note: 'To earthy' is a slip in this printing of Storr; read 'to earth'. The Greek has the earth hitting back, ἀντιτύπᾳ (l. 134, _antitypai_, 'that returns the blow'), and the rare participle τανταλωθεὶς (_tantalotheis_), 'swung through the air', in which a Greek ear probably heard the name of Tantalus, another man who presumed on the gods. The second pair of stanzas begins here, with the fall.

s2.quote: The fire-brand from his impious hand was dashed,
s2.note: In the Greek he is 'the fire-bearer' (l. 135), and that is all. 'Impious' is Storr's comment. The Greek does not need to say it: the man carrying fire against Thebes is answered by the god's fire, and the title he bears is the title of his punishment.

s2.quote: As like a Bacchic reveler on he came,
s2.note: βακχεύων (l. 136, _bakcheuon_), 'raving like a bacchant', in a mad onrush. Look where the word falls. Bacchus is the god of Thebes, his mother was Theban, and at the end of this same song the elders ask him to lead their dance (l. 154). Yet the first Bacchic thing in the play is the frenzy of the city's attacker. The god's madness is on both sides of the wall, and that is a warning about the god they are about to call on again in [[s12]].

s2.quote: Outbreathing hate and flame,
s2.note: 'With the blasts of most hateful winds': ἐχθίστων ἀνέμων (l. 137). ἐχθίστων (_echthiston_) is the superlative of _echthros_, and we have just heard Antigone use the comparative of her own sister (l. 86). For the elders the word is easy. The enemy is the man outside the gates with a torch. The prologue has already shown us someone for whom the line between own and enemy runs through the family and through the city.

s2.quote: Here, there, great Area like a war-horse wheeled;
s2.note: 'Area' is a misprint for Ares: μέγας Ἄρης (l. 139). 'War-horse' is vague where the Greek is exact. Ares is δεξιόσειρος (l. 140, _dexioseiros_), the right-hand trace-horse of a four-horse chariot team, the strong one on the outside that does the work on the turn. An Athenian audience knew chariot-racing well. The god of war is the horse that brings the team round, and the enemy's line turns with him.

s2.quote: Seven captains at our seven gates
s2.note: Seven captains at seven gates, posted 'equals against equals' (ll. 141-142). This is the matched catalogue of Aeschylus's Seven against Thebes compressed into two lines, and the audience would supply the rest. 'Equals against equals' is the phrase to hold: it applies to six pairs as a boast and to the seventh as a horror.

s2.quote: Trophy for Zeus who turns the fight;
s2.note: Ζηνὶ τροπαίῳ (l. 143), Zeus 'of the rout'. A trophy, _tropaion_, is by origin the monument set up at the spot where the enemy turned, _trope_, and ran. Storr's 'who turns the fight' gets the etymology. The six defeated captains leave their bronze to the god. The seventh pair leave nothing to anybody.

s2.quote: Save two alone, that ill-starred pair
s2.note: τοῖν στυγεροῖν (l. 144, _toin stygeroin_), in the dual again: 'the two abhorred ones'. Storr's 'ill-starred' is softer than the Greek, which means hateful, abominable. The important thing is that it covers both of them. Before Creon has said a word, the elders do not distinguish patriot from traitor; the brothers are one pair with one adjective. It is the edict in the next scene that divides them, and Antigone's whole case is that they should not be divided.

s2.quote: One mother to one father bare,
s2.note: 'Of one father and one mother' (ll. 144-145). In [[s5]] Antigone answers Creon's 'was the other not also your brother?' with almost these words: of one mother and the same father. The Chorus has made her argument for her before she appears, without noticing. In this house, too, 'one father and one mother' is never an innocent phrase.

s2.quote: Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
s2.note: 'Drave' is the old past tense of drive. The Greek ends on κοινοῦ θανάτου (l. 147), 'a common death' in which both have their share: _koinon_ once more, the first word of the play (l. 1) and Ismene's word for the brothers' doom (l. 57). Their spears are δικρατεῖς (l. 146), 'both victorious', each one killing its man. And this is all the victory song has to say about the event that made Creon king and that drives the whole play: a few lines, then on to the dancing.

s2.quote: Now Victory to Thebes returns again
s2.note: Victory in person, 'great of name', has come to Thebes 'of the many chariots' (ll. 148-149), answering the city's joy with her own. The stanza opens in Greek with a brisk 'but enough', turning away from the brothers. The turn is too quick, and I think we are meant to feel that it is.

s2.quote: Memories of war blot out.
s2.note: In the line before, 'should' is a misprint for 'shout'. The elders propose θέσθαι λησμοσύναν (l. 151, _lesmosynan_), 'to make a forgetting' of the war just over. That is the wish the play refuses. There is a body on the plain that cannot be forgotten, a ruler who will not let it be forgotten, and a girl who will not forget it either. Of the three parties the Chorus is the one that would like to move on, and that tells us a good deal about how it will behave under pressure.

s2.quote: Dance and sing the live night long.
s2.note: 'With all-night dances', at every temple of the gods (ll. 152-153). 'Live night' is Storr's 'livelong'. None of it happens. By the time this day ends the altars they mean to visit are fouled with scraps of the unburied corpse, as Teiresias reports in [[s11]], and the house they serve has three more dead in it.

s2.quote: Bacchus, shaker of the ground!
s2.note: Βάκχιος (l. 154) is to lead the dance, and he is ἐλελίχθων (l. 153, _elelichthon_), 'earth-shaker', the one whose dancers make the ground of Thebes tremble. This is the first of two invocations. The second is the desperate hymn of [[s12]], when the elders beg him to come with healing foot to a city sick with pollution. Having heard his name used for Capaneus's frenzy forty lines ago, we should not assume his coming is always gentle.

s2.quote: Lo! Creon our new lord draws near,
s2.note: The anapaests return to announce an entrance. The elders call him βασιλεὺς χώρας (l. 155), 'king of the land', where Antigone called him only the general (l. 8). But they say 'new' twice in two lines: νεοχμὸς (l. 156, _neochmos_) and νεαραῖσι (l. 157), a new ruler by new turns of fortune. _Neochmos_ can carry a hint of the novel and untried. He is introduced as a novelty before he opens his mouth.

s2.quote: Crowned by this strange chance, our king.
s2.note: A cool way to announce a monarch. Creon holds the throne because both heirs died yesterday, and everything he does in [[s3]] is done by a man one day into the job and anxious to look equal to it. Storr's 'strange chance' leaves out one thing: in Greek the chances are the gods' (l. 157), 'fortunes sent by the gods'. The elders see heaven's hand in his accession. That is a title he can lose in the same way.

s2.quote: What, I marvel, pondering?
s2.note: Literally 'what plan is he rowing': μῆτιν ἐρέσσων (l. 158, _metin eresson_), plying a scheme as one plies an oar. Storr's 'pondering' drops the boat. It matters because Creon's first words in [[s3]] are about the city as a ship that the gods have righted after a storm, and the ship of state is his master image. The elders' metaphor hands him his opening.

s2.quote: Us, his elders, one and all,
s2.note: The meeting is σύγκλητον (l. 160, _synkleton_), 'specially convened', the Athenian term for an extraordinary session, and it is a λέσχην (l. 161, 'council') of γερόντων, old men. They have been called κοινῷ κηρύγματι (l. 161b), 'by a common proclamation'. Both words are from the prologue: _kerygma_ was Antigone's word for the edict (l. 8) and _koinon_ the first word she spoke. So the play sets two summonses side by side. Antigone called one sister outside the gates to hear in private; Creon calls the elders by herald to hear in public. Neither of them is asking for advice.
